surfaces.part: ice floor (horizontal surface seen from above)

answer.evidence: This is a room with a dark rock back wall (rows 15-47, about 33 rows of vertical face) above a large ice floor (rows 48 to roughly 160) that is seen from above. The wall is capped only by a thin grey lip at rows 12-14, which reads as a rim with a darker band below it at rows 15-19. The side walls are 1-px outline strips with no top surface, and the bottom edge is a thin line. The floor gives a large horizontal surface and the back wall gives a front face, so the room reads as 3/4. The wall tops themselves are only a rim, not real top surfaces.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a room interior: an ice floor with a thin dark rock band on top, framed by a near-black border. It is not a building with roof, walls and door, so the kind only loosely matches. The measured facts count against it. Median colours per tile are 7, against 18 and 11 for the references. Total colours are 57, against 185 and 66. Dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references. This matches the visible heavy black frame, which gives a uniform sticker-like outline instead of dark material-tone edges. The ice floor does carry dithering, cracks and speckle, so flat-fill coverage is only 1% and texture is some. The ramps are shallow, about 4 light-blue steps on the ice and 3-4 on the rock band. The rock band is small and murky, and its stones are not shaded one by one as in the stone reference. Overall it is thinner and flatter than the references, and the neutral black outline is the decisive weakness.

surfaces.part: back wall top cap (thin gray strip)

answer.evidence: This is a room tile, not a gate, pavilion or building. The top strip (rows 12-14) is a thin gray band, 3 rows at most, with a lighter first row and a darker row below. It acts as an outline or rim, not a real wall-top surface. Below it the brown rock wall (rows 15-47) is a plain vertical face with no roof or lintel top slope. Rows 48-175 are a very large flat ice floor seen straight down, with no front face or volume of its own. The side walls are 1-column vertical lines with no top surface. Overall it is a back wall in elevation above a top-down floor slab, not a 3/4 volume with a roof or top plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is an ice floor with a rock-wall band, surrounded by a near-black frame. The ice floor has dithering, cracks and mottling in about 4 blue steps, which gives decent texture. The rock wall band is dark and murky, with only about 3-4 brown steps and little tile-by-tile shading. Measured facts: 100% of dark edge pixels are neutral (references 7-9%), so the outline and frame read as a neutral black sticker line rather than a tinted material tone. Median colours per tile is 7, against 18 and 11 for the references, and total colours is 57 against 185 and 66. Flat-fill coverage is 1%, so flat fills are not the problem. The piece has no roof, door or windows, so it is structurally much simpler than the references. Overall it is lower in density, with a neutral black border, and does not meet the Beodeul bar.

surfaces.part: ice floor (open room interior seen from above)

answer.evidence: Rows 0-11 are dark background. Rows 12-14 are a thin 3-row gray cap that fades from L134 to L78. That is only a rim, not a real wall top surface. Rows 15-47 are the rock wall's vertical south face, 33 rows tall, with a dark shadow band at rows 44-47. Rows 48 to about 160 are a large ice floor seen from above, like contents inside an open room. It has a thin outline on the left, right and bottom edges. The room reads as a floor plane under a back wall face. The wall's own top surface is only a rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a room interior (ice floor, rock-wall band, dark frame), not a building with roof, walls and door, so it does not match the reference kind. Measured facts: 7 colours per tile against 18 and 11 for the references, 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66, and 100% neutral dark edge pixels against 7% and 9%. The frame and outline are neutral near-black, which is the sticker look; Beodeul uses tinted dark material tones. The ice floor has dither and crack texture, but it is only about 3-4 pale blue steps. The rock band at the top has some variation but is dark and muddy with few steps. Flat-fill coverage is low (1%), but overall the piece is shallower than both references in density and outline craft.

answer.evidence: The whole sprite is a full-width 192px rectangle, not a standing object. At the top is a thin gray wall-cap band (rows 12-14, light row 12 fading darker) with dark shadow below (rows 15-21). Below it is a vertical brown rock wall face (rows ~22-47), which is the only front face. The rest, rows 48-175, is a large flat ice floor texture seen straight down. It has no front face, roof slope, or ellipse. The wall top is only a 3-row rim, and the floor is a top-down slab. The result is a room tile (back wall plus floor), not a building or gate with a visible roof or lintel top surface, so the structure kind does not fit well.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is an ice-cave room, not a house with roof, walls and door, but it is judged on its structure and shading. The ice floor has pleasant dithering, crack lines and several blue lightness steps (about 4-5), and flat-fill coverage is only 1%. However, the measurements show the candidate is shallower than the references. Median colours per tile are 7 against 18 and 11 for the references, and there are 57 distinct colours against 185 and 66. 100% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references. The thick near-black frame around the room and the neutral dark band under the wall strip are the 'sticker' outline look, not a dark tone of the adjacent material. The rock wall band is dark and muddy, with only about 3-4 brown steps and little per-stone shading. The room is mostly one ice-floor material with a thin wall strip, so it has fewer material ramps than the roof, plaster and stone of the references. Overall it is flatter and more sticker-like than the Beodeul standard.
